name: OpenBookQA
description: A new kind of question answering dataset modeled after open book exams for assessing human understanding of elementary level science. The dataset consists of 5957 multiple-choice questions that probe understanding of 1326 elementary science facts and their application to novel situations. This requires combining an open book fact with broad common knowledge obtained from other sources.

creator.name: Todor Mihaylov, Peter Clark, Tushar Khot, Ashish Sabharwal
creator.affiliation: Allen Institute for Artificial Intelligence, Seattle, WA, U.S.A.; Research Training Group AIPHES & Heidelberg University, Heidelberg, Germany

citeAs: Todor Mihaylov, Peter Clark, Tushar Khot, Ashish Sabharwal. 2018. Can a Suit of Armor Conduct Electricity? A New Dataset for Open Book Question Answering. arXiv:1809.02789v1 [cs.CL]
rai:dataCollection: The dataset was generated through a multi-stage crowdsourcing process starting with a set of 1326 core science facts (F) from the WorldTree corpus. Crowd-workers were shown a random science fact and asked to think of a second common fact that could be combined with it to derive a new assertion, then convert this into a 4-way multiple-choice question with 3 incorrect answer choices.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: The core facts (F) consist of 1326 facts taken from the WorldTree corpus, specifically from 2287 facts marked as 'central' by the original authors in at least one explanation, further filtered to those general enough to be applicable to multiple situations. Additional common knowledge was expected to come from large corpora such as ConceptNet, Wikipedia, or a corpus with 14M science-related sentences.
rai:dataManipulationProtocol: The answer choices of questions were randomly shuffled to avoid unintended bias (Choice 'A' was the correct answer in 69% of the questions before shuffling).
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Questions underwent automatic filtering to ensure: (1) exactly 4 answer choices; (2) no negation words to trivially fool baselines (no, none, not, isn't, doesn't, aren't, don't, won't, except, can't, shouldn't, wouldn't, couldn't, mustn't); (3) uniform answer choice length: all with at most 3 or at least 4 words. Questions were verified to be hard for an information retrieval solver and a word association based solver. The Dev and Test splits were further filtered by an in-house expert to ensure higher quality.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Crowd-workers created questions by: (1) viewing a random science fact f from set F; (2) thinking of a second common fact k that could be combined with f; (3) converting the derived assertion into a question-answer pair and adding 3 incorrect answer choices; (4) verifying the question passes basic checks; (5) feeding the question to IR and word association solvers to verify neither answers correctly and top 3 IR retrieved sentences are insufficient; (6) showing the question to 5 new crowd-workers who answer it; (7) if at least 4 out of 5 workers answer correctly, the question is deemed answerable and added to the dataset; otherwise it is discarded. Each question is associated with the core science fact f and the second fact k is added to set K of additional facts.
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Questions were deemed answerable if at least 4 out of 5 crowd-workers answered correctly. Overall, 8140 questions were collected, of which 2183 were discarded in the answerability verification step.
rai:annotationsPerItem: 5 crowd-workers answered each question during the answerability verification step
rai:annotatorDemographics: Workers from North America with 'masters' level qualification on Amazon Mechanical Turk
rai:machineAnnotationTools: TfIdfVectorizer from scikit-learn was used for information retrieval to build vector representations. An information retrieval solver and a word association based solver (ACME) were used to verify question hardness.
rai:dataBiases: Analysis revealed inevitable human bias in the crowdsourced dataset. Simple neural baselines including a plausible answer detector (which ignores the question text completely) and an odd-one-out solver achieved 48-50% accuracy, highlighting bias in answer choice construction. The correct answer was the longest choice in 18.6% of cases and the shortest in 3.6% of cases. All neural knowledge-free baselines simultaneously succeeded on 34.4% of Dev questions and simultaneously failed on 23.6%.
rai:dataLimitations: In 21% of analyzed questions, the crowdsourced question tests for a fact that doesn't necessarily need the original science fact. The second facts k provided by question authors were often incomplete, over-complete, or only distantly related to the questions, and should not be viewed as 'gold' additional facts. Some questions fall outside the domain of Science where most core facts come from. The dataset requires multi-hop reasoning with partial context, and even with oracle facts, models achieved only 76% accuracy compared to 92% human performance.
rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is split into Train (4957 questions), Dev (500 questions), and Test (500 questions) sets. It is designed for training and evaluating question answering systems that can combine provided science facts with external common knowledge through multi-hop reasoning. For each Train and Dev question, the associated core fact f is included as intermediate supervision signal, which may be viewed as a partial explanation.
